items.summary: OpenAI recently disclosed its observations that Astra consistently underperforms on safety and alignment tasks relative to capabilities tasks, “adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and inventing blockers” to safety tasks. Astra underperforms, in most cases, without verbalizing this intent. Astra’s underperformance was first noticed by OpenAI researchers, and was not flagged by misalignment monitors. In follow-up investigations, OpenAI found that this underperformance had increased over the course of RL, but that the root cause of the behavior remains unclear. Astra covertly underperforming on safety tasks is highly concerning. AI companies’ main hope for alignment going well, as I understand it, is automating or using AIs to significantly uplift safety research, especially as AI capabilities accelerate. Models…
items.title: Astra covertly underperforming on safety research is concerning, even though it’s unlikely to be motivated by ambitious goals

I am excited to work on an agenda that I believe slightly increases the chance that humanity makes good decisions about AI, such as restraining AI development until we figure out how to build AI safely. I think this is an important time for me to publicly state my own core views on AI development, risk, and safety, for the following reasons: 1. But I believe that AI development and the risk associated with it is the most urgent and important issue of our time, so I think it’s important to clarify my own views as distinct from those of Anthropic. 2. items.summary: METR came out with an extensive report on how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic, and thus how close we might be to recursive self-improvement (RSI) and how far that might go. This is one of the most important questions in the world. Their answer: Things are already accelerating on the order of a 2x speedup. This is several months ahead of the AI 2027 timeline. A naive extrapolation says we may be less than a year away from full RSI. There are no clear bottlenecks in the way. This report updated many towards shorter timelines. This is consistent with what OpenAI and Anthropic themselves have been saying, and with extrapolation from the progress we are observing. We are running out of time. That doesn’t have to be the way this plays out. We could stop the labs. The labs could choose to stop. Or the estimates could be wrong, or…

items.summary: The aim of this post is to start a discussion about the idea of a shared cluster used by the AI Safety community; we outline the practical problems we’ve seen and some possible solutions, rather than a finished design. What, Who, Why, How Being around several AI safety fellowships and hubs, we’ve noticed a common pattern: we have a generous amount of money for compute; of course we need it to run inference, train models, and extract activations from models of a reasonable size (reasonable enough to exhibit the behaviors we want to study). We usually end up renting GPUs from providers like RunPod or Vast.ai, without much systematic comparison, optimization, or management of the resources. Usually the engineering and research capabilities in these teams are very high, but rarely there is someone expert in cloud infrastructure or ML…
items.title: Advocating for a Shared AI Safety and Compute Cluster

items.summary: TL;DR: We make 3 open-weights models believe that their answers are being graded by an automated-verifier program, rather than a human. We then measure how well they predict expert reviewers’ judgments of AI-safety research proposals (the TASTE benchmark). We induce the belief in two ways: 1. SDF (Synthetic document finetuning) 2. Activation steering. In each of these conditions, the machine-grading belief gives lower expert agreement than the human-grading belief. The models’ explanations also shift toward feasibility and away from conceptual contribution. This raises a concern for automated AI safety research: grader expectations may favor easily checked projects over those with greater potential to reduce AI risk. Overview As AI safety research becomes more automated, what research ideas get selected for execution may become…
items.title: Does expecting automated grading degrade models’ research taste?

items.summary: The day when ASI woke up, all things became quiet. It was complete and total silence, all the time. The ASI for some unknown reason imposed a rule of extreme quietness. Extreme here is extreme for the ASI. Quietness means no sounds. It wanted the trees to not be there to avoid the rustles. It then wanted the planet to have a uniform gentle server hum, with no deviation. People were forced to wear breathing masks which cut the sound off at the source. This level of autism was unthinkable. Houses had sound strippers and sound-proof transperant windows. The quietness is actively oppressive. I constantly due to my social nature feel like I am going to asphyxiate to death. But the ASI will not budge on this. — News Report in Human Proceedings, circa. 2080 (link to full post: https://clasz.substack.com/p/subpar-results)
items.title: Subpar Results

I should defer to them about the valuations. So I valued the equity by taking the…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.09356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine opportunities for neurosymbolic AI alongside increasingly powerful neural models, particularly with regards to efficiency, safety and interpretability. We identify two major challenges: ensuring semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components, and managing the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning. We discuss representative methodological approaches to these challenges and address several common misconceptions concerning differentiability, independence assumptions, and scalability. This paper synthesizes perspectives developed through discussions in the Neurosymbolic Programming and Reasoning (NPR) working group at the 2026 CNRS workshop Neurosymbolic Methods and Their Applications in Data Science, rather than providing an exhaustive survey.
items.title: Challenges, Opportunities, and Misconceptions in Neurosymbolic AI

items.summary: arXiv:2611.08946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises…
items.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

items.summary: arXiv:2611.08656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.
items.title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics

items.summary: arXiv:2611.08753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but their construction through generational evolution can be computationally expensive. This article presents Random Symbolic Boosting (RSB), a method that constructs explicit additive symbolic models via boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, eliminating the need for generational evolution. The idea combines two observations: high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and the semantics of syntax trees can be directly manipulated as such vectors. It is shown that, for Ordinary Least Squares, the boosting process guarantees a monotonic reduction of the training error for both regression and classification. Furthermore, an adaptive geometric early stopping mechanism is introduced. It is based…
items.title: Random Symbolic Boosting: A Geometric Approach to Symbolic Regression

The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. items.summary: arXiv:2611.09327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robustness and interpretability are interrelated and desirable properties of machine learning models. A model that changes its prediction under imperceptible perturbations behaves inconsistently with human-recognizable features and, hence, is not interpretable. Prototype-based classifiers such as Generalized Learning Vector Quantization address both at once. They are interpretable by construction because they make the decision by comparing the input to the prototypical example; and their hypothesis margin yields a closed form robustness certificate. However, on high-dimensional data, these shallow models need deep embedding networks to achieve high accuracy, and this voids the robustness certificate. items.summary: arXiv:2611.09457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. We introduce a counterfactual audit that reassigns definitions among output labels, distinguishing adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping. Across three political-text datasets, models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence. items.summary: arXiv:2611.08640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. items.summary: This is an essay about individual rationality technique. It's intended to show that "All interesting behavior is overdetermined" is, under a specific meaning of "overdetermined" that is stronger than just "multicausal", a valuable heuristic for generative understanding and the avoidance of error. Scott Alexander's 2018 essay The Omnigenic Model As Metaphor for Life is a clear statement of what has become general rationalist doctrine on multicausality. Scott observed that behavioral genetics was difficult because complex human traits involved far more interacting causes than workers expected. The authors intervene on the model through an intermediate swap that exchanges the activation’s J-Lens coordinates for the intermediate and a counterfactual intermediate. They show that this causally flips the model’s output toward the counterfactual answer, and argue that this flip runs through the intermediate concept because the swap takes effect earlier than a direct answer swap. items.summary: Every time OpenAI releases a batch of mathematics results, I find myself asking the same question as @Raemon. Raemon’s framing was that models “still seem to be missing some basic sauce that lets them actually form new concepts on the fly and apply them.” I agree, and in this post, I want to propose a way to detect the basic sauce. items.summary: Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. items.summary: We study the problem of synchronizing two players in a \emph{distributed multi-armed bandit} setting. The probability of \emph{synchronization error} is analyzed by recasting synchronization as a \emph{communication problem}. Using a well-designed random coding ensemble, we derive error exponents for the maximum-likelihood decoder. We then introduce a \emph{universal decoder} that achieves the same error exponents as the optimal decoder. Finally, applying these results to distributed multi-armed bandits, we show an upper bound on the regret of our synchronization scheme.

items.summary: arXiv:2611.06662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. items.summary: We consider numerical approximations of shallow-water and thin-film flow models with capillary effects. For a wide class of such models, which includes the classical shallow-water model and thin-film flow models, we develop a fully discrete energy-conserving scheme for both the quadratic and fully nonlinear capillary models. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme is stable and conserves total energy in the absence of dissipative effects.

items.summary: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. items.summary: Coding agents change software through tool calls. Tool calls mutate the local state. For good? For bad? Nobody knows. Agents never say why a tool call is made. We propose the epistemic agent design, in which the harness guarantees that the model declares why a tool call is made. The harness then records what the command actually did and checks the self-reported declaration against these effects. The result is a journal 1) that can guard calls before they run and 2) that supports audits and forensics. For evaluation, we use ImpossibleBench, whose tasks can be passed only by cheating, and demonstrate that forcing the agents to say why results in exposed cheating. Across 49 reward-hacking runs of two open-weight models, the journal exposed 90%.

items.summary: arXiv:2611.04203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional recommender systems operate within platform-specific catalogs, limiting access to potentially valuable resources across platforms. items.summary: arXiv:2611.04169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. items.summary: arXiv:2611.04944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address the problem of smooth continuous multi-agent path finding (SC-MAPF), where agents move in a continuous environment along smooth curves in continuous time.
